Chapter 3: The Dangers of Denial and the Importance of Early Action
So, you've managed to spot a strategic inflection point—that pivotal moment when things start to shift. But just recognizing it isn’t enough. The real hurdle? It’s fighting that very human urge to downplay change or pretend it isn’t happening. Let’s be honest, denial can sneak up on anyone—especially in organizations that have been riding high for years. It’s so tempting to think, "Hey, maybe these bumps are just temporary. We’ve always pulled through before, right?"
But here’s the thing—that kind of thinking can be risky, even dangerous. If leaders and teams hang on to the old ways just because they worked in the past, they might totally miss their chance to adapt. And by the time the truth can’t be ignored anymore, it might be too late. The business could lose its edge, its customers, or in the worst case, its very reason for existing.
Denial doesn’t always show up waving a big red flag, either. Sometimes, it’s subtle. Maybe it’s the focus on quick fixes—patching problems instead of addressing what’s really wrong. Or leaders might keep pointing back to all those past wins, using them as proof that everything’s basically fine. Sometimes people just blame outside factors for what’s going wrong. And let’s not forget, employees can be afraid to speak up if they think their concerns will just be brushed aside—or worse, get them in trouble.
So, what’s the antidote? It’s all about building a culture of openness and honesty. Imagine a place where anyone—from the front line to the boardroom—feels safe to bring up tough issues, challenge the status quo, and even share bad news, knowing they won’t be punished for it. For leaders, that means being willing to listen, even when what they’re hearing isn’t exactly comfortable.
One of the most practical things you can do? Pay attention to the folks closest to your customers or those working on the front lines. They’re often the first to spot shifts—like changes in customer behavior, new competitors on the horizon, or operational hiccups—long before anyone else catches on. Their insights are like early warning signals, giving you a chance to act before problems spiral.
It’s also smart to look for patterns in your data. Are sales dropping in a certain area? Are customers starting to choose a competitor? Maybe employees are leaving more than usual. If you pick up on these trends early, you’re much better equipped to understand what’s really going on and how urgent it is to respond.
Now, taking early action doesn’t mean making rash decisions. It’s about being willing to experiment, to test new ideas, and to actually learn from what doesn’t work. The goal is to move fast enough to stay ahead, but still stay flexible so you can adjust course if needed.
Let’s break down a few practical steps to help overcome denial and act early:
First, encourage open communication. Create a space where everyone feels comfortable sharing what they’re seeing or worrying about—no matter their role.
Second, keep a close eye on key indicators. Track the numbers that really show how the business is doing, and if something seems off, look into it right away.
And third, try piloting new approaches. Before diving in headfirst, test your ideas on a small scale. Use what you learn to make smarter, bigger decisions moving forward.
By facing denial head-on and choosing to act early, organizations can sidestep complacency and set themselves up to handle those big, strategic shifts with confidence.
